items.prompt: What does a passing test tell you?
choices: The code works at every possible scale
It works in the cases the tests ran
The code has no bugs left in it
items.explanation: A test is a sample of cases. It speaks for those cases only.

items.prompt: You tested a 10 cm toothpick bridge with one coin. What does that test say about a 15 cm bridge?
choices: It will sag exactly as much as the short one
It will sag exactly half again as much
Nothing directly, that case was never tested
items.explanation: The test only covered the 10 cm span. Anything about 15 cm needs a model.

items.prompt: Which of these is a prediction question?
choices: How will this behave at ten times the traffic?
Does this function return the right sum for 2 and 3?
items.explanation: Prediction asks about a case not yet observed. The other two ask about code that exists now.

items.prompt: Math used as prediction means doing what?
choices: Proving that a program contains no bugs of any kind
Forecasting an untried case from a known formula
Counting how many lines of code a team wrote down
items.explanation: The idea is relationship plus numbers gives a forecast.

items.prompt: Which tool answers 'does this compile'?
items.explanation: Compilers check consistency of code. They do not forecast load.

items.prompt: You have no data at all and want a rough size of something. Which tool fits?
choices: An exact formula with measured inputs
A load test on the real system
items.explanation: Fermi estimation gets an order of magnitude from almost nothing.

items.prompt: You have measured numbers and a known relationship between them. Which tool fits?
items.explanation: With real inputs and a trusted relationship, plug them in for a specific, checkable number.

items.prompt: Why can a test suite stay green while production breaks at higher load?
choices: The tests are always wrong at scale
The tests never created that load
items.explanation: A green suite means the cases it ran passed. Load beyond those cases was never exercised.

items.prompt: A service passes every unit test and type check, ships, and then misses its latency target after traffic grows by half. What kind of question was never asked?
choices: What happens at a load nobody had tried yet
Whether each function returns correct values
Whether the code compiles on the build server
Whether the tests were written before the code
items.explanation: The tests and compiler answered correctness. Nothing in them forecast behaviour at a bigger load, so the miss was a prediction gap.
items.reference:
Two different questions
✅ test, compiler: does it work in the case I ran?
🔮 formula plus numbers: what happens in a case I have not run?
🌉 tested 10 cm bridge says nothing about a 15 cm one
🧮 no data: Fermi estimate. real numbers: known formula
Why: a test covers the cases it ran; only a model with real numbers speaks about the cases you have not reached yet.
items.learnMore:
Correctness math vs. predictive math

Tests and type checkers confirm a program is consistent with what it claims. Predictive math takes a relationship you trust and the numbers you have, and forecasts a case nobody has run, such as ten times the traffic.

Common mistake

Reading a green test suite as a promise about conditions the tests never created.
items.reflection: Think of something you checked once and then relied on in a bigger situation (a recipe doubled, a route on a busy day). What did the first check not cover?

items.prompt: A teammate says, 'We load-tested at 100 users, so 1,000 will be fine.' What should you ask first?
choices: Whether 100 users is a round enough number
Whether the test was run on a weekday
Whether the testers used the newest browser
How the result changes as the load grows
items.explanation: The claim extrapolates a tested point to a case ten times larger. Whether that is safe depends on how result grows with load.

items.prompt: 'Twice the users means twice the load' is an example of what?
items.explanation: It assumes the result scales by the same factor as the input.

items.prompt: Each of 10 users can message each of the other 9. How many possible conversations is that?
items.explanation: 10 x 9 = 90, one for each user-and-other-user pair.

items.prompt: Each of 100 users can message each of the other 99. How many possible conversations?
For a loaded beam, sag grows with length cubed. A bridge 1.5 times as long sags about how much more?
items.explanation: 1.5 cubed is 3.375, so about 3.4 times.

items.prompt: What is the first question to ask before assuming a result scales linearly?
choices: How long did the test take?
items.explanation: What is counted decides how fast it grows.

items.prompt: For the same beam, a span twice as long sags about how many times as much?
items.explanation: 2 cubed is 8.

items.prompt: Users grew from 10 to 100. Conversations grew from 90 to 9,900. Conversations grew about how many times?
items.explanation: 9,900 divided by 90 is 110.

items.prompt: Which relationship really is linear?
choices: A flat price per item times the number of items
Sag of a loaded beam against how long its span is
Possible chat pairs against user count
items.explanation: A fixed cost per item doubles exactly when the count doubles. The other two bend.

items.prompt: A toothpick bridge twice as long as the tested one is built. Sag grows with the cube of length. About how many times as much does it sag?
items.explanation: Sag scales with length cubed, so doubling the span gives 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 times the sag.
items.reference:
When is 'twice the input, twice the result' false?
📏 flat price per item: linear, safe to scale
🌉 sag grows with length cubed: 1.5x long, 3.4x sag
💬 everyone messages everyone: 10 users 90 pairs, 100 users 9,900
❓ first ask what is being counted
Why: many real relationships bend, so a percentage change in the input is not the same percentage change in the result.
items.learnMore:
The linear trap

A linear guess scales the result by the same factor as the input. It is right for flat per-item costs and wrong whenever the thing counted grows faster, such as pairs of users or beam sag with span.

Common mistake

Calibrating intuition on small sizes and applying it unchanged to much larger ones.
items.reflection: Where in your own work or daily life does doubling something cost more than double (a meeting, a commute, a group chat)? What is being counted there?

items.prompt: A chat room doubles from 20 users to 40, and every user can message every other. Roughly how many times more possible conversations are there?
items.explanation: 20 x 19 = 380 and 40 x 39 = 1,560. The ratio is a little over 4, close to the square of the user ratio, not the ratio itself.

items.prompt: In L = λW, what does L stand for?
choices: The average number inside the system
items.explanation: L counts how many items are inside on average.

items.prompt: In L = λW, what does λ stand for?
items.explanation: λ is how many arrive per unit of time.

items.prompt: 100 requests arrive per second and each stays 0.2 seconds. How many are in flight on average?
10 customers arrive per hour and each stays half an hour. How many are inside on average?
Per second times seconds leaves what kind of quantity?
items.explanation: The seconds cancel, leaving how many things.

items.prompt: Must traffic be perfectly regular for Little's Law to hold?
choices: Yes, arrivals must be evenly spaced
No, any stable system obeys it
Yes, but only for web servers
items.explanation: The law holds for any stable system regardless of the arrival pattern.

items.prompt: 30 tickets arrive per day and each stays open 2 days. How many are open on average?
Arrivals stay the same but the average stay doubles. What happens to the number inside?
items.explanation: L is proportional to W when λ is fixed.

items.prompt: A service receives 400 requests per second and each takes 100 ms on average. How many requests are in flight on average?
items.reference:
Little's Law: things inside = arrivals x stay
🚪 λ: arrivals per unit of time
⏱️ W: average time each one stays
📦 L = λ x W: how many are inside on average
🏪 200 per hour x 0.25 hours = 50 inside
Why: the count inside is the arrival rate times the average stay, and the units (per second x seconds) leave a plain count.
items.learnMore:
Little's Law

For any stable system, average number inside equals arrival rate times average time inside. It does not care about the shape of the traffic or what flows through: requests, tickets and customers all follow it.

Common mistake

Mixing time units, such as an arrival rate per hour with a stay measured in minutes.
items.reflection: Pick a place where people or things queue in your life (a cafe, an inbox, a lift). What are its arrival rate and its average stay, and roughly how many are inside right now?

items.prompt: In the wait formula, what does ρ (rho) mean?
choices: The number of requests per second
The fraction of time the server is busy
items.explanation: ρ is utilization, from 0 to 1.

items.prompt: What is ρ / (1 - ρ) when ρ = 0.5?
What is ρ / (1 - ρ) when ρ = 0.9?
As utilization approaches 100%, what happens to the wait?
items.explanation: 1 - ρ approaches 0, so the ratio becomes huge.

items.prompt: How much room is left at 80% busy?
Going from 60% to 90% busy, the wait gets about how much longer?
items.explanation: 9 divided by 1.5 is 6.

items.prompt: Which move adds more wait: 50% to 55%, or 90% to 95%?
items.explanation: Near the top, the same few points cost far more: 9 becomes 19.

items.prompt: Why does dividing by (1 - ρ) make the wait blow up?
choices: Because ρ itself grows without limit
Because computers slow down when busy
items.explanation: Dividing by a number close to zero gives a very large result.

items.prompt: A team at 70% utilization plans for traffic that would reach 90%. Roughly how much longer does the average wait get?
items.explanation: 70% gives 2.33 and 90% gives 9. The ratio 9 / 2.33 is about 3.9.
items.reference:
Wait grows like ρ / (1 - ρ)
50% busy: 0.5 / 0.5 = 1
60% busy: 0.6 / 0.4 = 1.5
90% busy: 0.9 / 0.1 = 9
95% busy: 0.95 / 0.05 = 19
Why: the room left, 1 - ρ, shrinks toward zero, so dividing by it makes the wait climb faster than the utilization does.
items.learnMore:
Why waiting explodes near full capacity

A busy server queues new arrivals behind a growing backlog. The standard single-server approximation says average wait scales with ρ / (1 - ρ), where ρ is the fraction of time the server is busy.

Common mistake

Treating a move from 60% to 90% as a move of 1.5 times when the wait itself moves about six times.
items.reflection: Think of a road, a shop or an inbox that works fine until it is nearly full. At what point does a little extra load suddenly make everything feel much worse?

items.prompt: Which single move adds the most wait?
items.explanation: The curve values go 1 to 1.5, 2.33 to 4, 4 to 9, and 9 to 19. The smallest step on the input adds the most, 10 units.

items.prompt: Today a service is 60% busy and traffic grows by 1.5 times. What is the projected utilization?
At 90% busy, how much room is left?
In the near-miss, how many times as long does the wait get?
items.explanation: 9 divided by 1.5 is 6.

items.prompt: 'Tight but survivable' in the near-miss was what kind of mistake?
choices: A linear read of a curved relationship
A typing mistake in the code
A wrong guess about the date
items.explanation: The utilization step was right. Reading the wait as 1.5 times was the linear error.

items.prompt: Which two numbers produce the 6x in the near-miss?
items.explanation: The wait curve gives 9 after growth and 1.5 before it.

items.prompt: Traffic grows 1.5 times. By roughly how much does the wait grow?
items.explanation: Traffic moves the service up the curve, where the wait multiplies far more.

items.prompt: What should the team do once the numbers show a 6x wait?
choices: Wait until next year as planned
items.explanation: The calculation shows the problem arrives before the full growth does.

items.prompt: Projected utilization is today's utilization times what?
items.explanation: More traffic with the same time per request keeps the server busier by that factor.

items.prompt: A service is 50% busy and traffic is forecast to grow 1.6 times. By the wait curve, how much longer is the average wait than today's?
items.explanation: 0.5 x 1.6 = 0.8 busy. Wait at 0.8 is 4, wait at 0.5 is 1, so the multiplier is 4.
items.reference:
The near-miss, step by step
🚦 today 60% busy: 0.6 / 0.4 = 1.5
📈 traffic x 1.5: 0.6 x 1.5 = 0.9 busy
🚨 at 90%: 0.9 / 0.1 = 9
⏱️ wait change: 9 / 1.5 = 6x from 1.5x traffic
Why: project the new utilization first, then read the wait off the curve at both ends and compare.
items.learnMore:
Working the capacity near-miss

Multiply today's utilization by the traffic growth to get the projected utilization, then compute the wait curve at both ends and divide. The result is the multiplier on wait, not a guess from percentages.

Common mistake

Stopping after the first multiplication and calling 90% survivable without reading the wait it implies.
items.reflection: Take a plan you made that scaled something up by a simple factor. Which second step, like the wait curve here, did you skip?

items.explanation: 0.4 x 2 = 0.8. Wait at 0.8 is 4 and at 0.4 is 0.4 / 0.6, about 0.67, and 4 / 0.67 is 6.

Working the capacity near-miss

Multiply today's utilization by the traffic growth to get the projected utilization, then compute the wait curve at both ends and divide. The result is the multiplier on wait, not a guess from percentages.

Common mistake

Stopping after the first multiplication and calling 90% survivable without reading the wait it implies.
items.reflection: Take a plan you made that scaled something up by a simple factor. Which second step, like the wait curve here, did you skip?

items.prompt: The numbers in these formulas describe what kind of values?
items.explanation: Both Little's Law and the wait curve use average rates and times.

items.prompt: What does 'headroom' mean here?
choices: Spare capacity beyond the average need
The physical height of the server cabinet
Free time the team has left over
items.explanation: Headroom absorbs bursts the average does not show.

items.prompt: What does 'steady state' mean?
choices: It is switched off for scheduled maintenance
It has settled into stable, average behaviour
The traffic is rising faster with every minute
items.explanation: Steady-state formulas describe a settled system.

items.prompt: Which can make each request slower under heavy load?
items.explanation: Waiting on shared resources adds to the time per request.

items.prompt: A flash sale causes a sharp spike. Is a steady-state formula enough on its own?
choices: No, a spike needs burst planning too
Yes, since averages already cover any spike
Yes, if the average is low
items.explanation: A spike is not the settled average the formula describes.

items.prompt: After computing a prediction, what is the next good step?
items.explanation: A prediction is a claim to be checked.

items.prompt: What is the risk of treating a formula's output as ground truth?
items.explanation: Real systems differ from clean assumptions in ways only measurement reveals.

items.prompt: Do formulas remove the need for headroom?
choices: No, they only narrow the uncertainty
items.explanation: Prediction reduces guesswork. Variation still needs spare room.

items.prompt: A team plans exactly to the average utilization its formula calls safe. Why can it still miss its latency target on some minutes?
choices: Bursts push the load up the steep curve
The formula was copied with a typing error
Average values cannot be used in formulas
Latency targets only apply at night
items.explanation: Real traffic varies around the average. During a burst a small extra load costs a lot of wait.
items.reference:
What a formula quietly assumes
📊 the inputs are averages: bursts are worse
⚙️ service time stays constant: contention raises it
⏳ steady state: a spike is a different problem
🔎 it is a prediction: compare it with measurements
Why: a correct calculation is only as true as its assumptions, so predict, then check against reality and keep headroom.
items.learnMore:
When a right formula gives a wrong answer

Averages hide bursts, constant service time rarely holds under load, and steady-state formulas do not describe a sudden spike. Use the formula to make a specific expectation, then measure and correct.

Common mistake

Treating the formula's output as ground truth and skipping the measurement.
items.reflection: Think of a forecast you trusted (weather, a deadline estimate). Which assumption behind it turned out to be false?

items.prompt: Each request gets slower as load rises, but the projection assumed constant time per request. What is the effect on the near-miss?
choices: True utilization is lower and the wait is better
Nothing changes because only traffic matters
The wait becomes exactly 6 times in every case
True utilization is higher and the wait is worse
items.explanation: Slower requests keep the server busy longer, so utilization lands above 0.9 and the wait is steeper than predicted.

items.prompt: A viral post sends a huge burst of traffic for ten minutes. Which hidden assumption is broken?
choices: That the formula uses averages at all
That wait is measured in seconds
That the system is in steady state
items.explanation: A short spike is not a settled average. It needs burst-capacity planning, not just a bigger average target.

items.prompt: Measured waits come out different from what the curve predicted. What is the best response?
choices: Trust the formula and discard the measurements
Treat it as information about a broken assumption
Trust the measurements and never use formulas
Average the two numbers and carry on
items.explanation: A mismatch shows which assumption failed. Correct the model with it, rather than discarding either side.
